name: Emeka Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Emeka. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be published with your name. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the press line at a metal stamping plant that makes brackets and back panels for washing machines. A coil of steel feeds into the press, the die comes down and punches out the shape, and I watch for split parts, change the coil when it runs out and keep the scrap bins clear. I've been there just over a year. I'm still learning die changes, which is the skilled part, and I'm not fast yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm, and I like that the plant pays on time every month. What wears me out is the noise, a press that big shakes your chest. On weekends I do welding in my uncle's garage, garden gates and railings for people in the area, and I use an AI app every day to price jobs, draw designs and answer customers. My girlfriend Ada teaches at the primary school, and we both go to my family's church on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a tool like any other, it just wasn't the miracle people said. The people who used it well still got ahead. I'd say that in the family group chat when my cousins start arguing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it suits me. The plant keeps paying, the gates business grows slowly, and I keep using the AI to do the paperwork faster than the competition. That's a good life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and put more weekends into the gates. I'd save up for my own welder instead of borrowing my uncle's, about two months of wages. And I'd keep learning die changes so I can ask for a raise next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How big is the gates business right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three or four jobs a month, mostly gates. The AI writes my quotes and sketches the design from a photo of the customer's driveway. People think I'm a big company. It's me and a garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave the plant for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd want both. The plant is security, the business is the future. My father always said don't put all your yams in one barn.

S0.say: It's a tool like any other, just not the miracle people said, and those who used it well still got ahead. I'd say that in the family group chat.
S0.think: It suits me: the plant keeps paying, the gates business grows, and AI helps me do paperwork faster than the competition.
S0.do: Keeps his plant job and puts more weekends into the gates business. Saves about two months of wages to buy his own welder. Keeps learning die changes to ask for a raise next year.
S0.quote: People think I'm a big company. It's me and a garage.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka already runs a small welding side business using AI daily for quotes and designs. He sees the plant as security and the business as the future. His father's sayings about not relying on one thing shape his caution as much as his ambition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who move early do well, and the people who wait for someone to save them don't. That's always been true. Companies have to modernise to survive, and I'd say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd see an opportunity. The press line will get more automated, sure. But small workshops like my uncle's garage will need help too, and I can bring them the tools I already use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the plant to train me on the new press controls and robots in the first year. I'd sign up for a welding certificate at the college, so the business is properly qualified. And I'd put more of my wage into the gates business, maybe buy a small plasma cutter that runs from a drawing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about any of the older men on the press line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them, yes. But I don't think the answer is the government paying them to sit at home. Better the company or the community helps them learn something. My church runs a skills evening, I'd help there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound very confident. Is it fair to say 'move early' to people who can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's harder for some people, I know. I'd tell them, come to the garage on Saturday, I'll show you what I do with the app. That's more use than a speech.

S1.say: People who move early do well and people who wait to be saved don't, as always. Companies have to modernise to survive.
S1.think: I'd see an opportunity: the press line automates, but small workshops will need help too, and I can bring them the tools I already use.
S1.do: Asks for training on new press controls and robots in the first year. Takes a welding certificate at the college. Puts more of his wage into the business and buys a plasma cutter that runs from a drawing.
S1.quote: Come to the garage on Saturday, I'll show you what I do with the app. That's more use than a speech.
S1.fieldNote: Emeka is confident and free-market, but his help for others is personal and local, through church and his garage, not government. He'd bring automation into his own business early. When pushed on fairness he softened but stuck to self-help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, nobody's coming to save you. Own something, learn the tools, look after your family. I'd say it in the group chat and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, two years is fast even for me. The plant goes, and if robots can weld and AI can design, then my gates business is up against the big firms with their own robots. My only chance is to own the machines myself, small, before everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a small welding robot or a plasma cutter with my savings and a loan from my uncle, in the first six months. I'd use AI to run the whole business side, quotes, orders, accounts. I'd keep the plant job as long as it lasted and put every spare penny into the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared exactly, more like running for a bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Spending savings on a robot when robots are everywhere, isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But doing nothing is a bigger risk. If I spend my savings and it fails, I'm broke at twenty-nine. If I do nothing, I'm broke at twenty-nine anyway, just slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That there's no time to learn properly. With longer, I'd do the certificates, build slowly. With two years, I'd have to buy first and learn after. That's not how my father did things, but my father didn't have this.

S2.say: Get ready, nobody's coming to save you: own something, learn the tools and look after your family. I'd say it in the group chat and at church.
S2.think: Two years is fast even for me, because the plant goes and my gates are up against big firms with robots. My only chance is to own the machines myself before everyone else does.
S2.do: Buys a small welding robot or plasma cutter within six months using savings and a loan from his uncle. Uses AI to run quotes, orders and accounts. Keeps the plant job while it lasts and puts every spare penny into the workshop.
S2.feel: Anxious, like running for a bus, but not frightened.
S2.quote: If I do nothing, I'm broke at twenty-nine anyway, just slower.
S2.fieldNote: His answer to fast AGI is to own machines, borrowing from family rather than seeking public help. He's clear-eyed that the bet could fail. The short warning forces him to buy first and learn after, breaking with his father's slow way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something if you start now. I'd tell the younger ones at church to learn a trade and the tools at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to do it properly. Get the welding certificate, grow the gates business, then buy the robot once I've got the customers to keep it busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the welding certificate in the first year. I'd move the business from my uncle's garage to a small unit by year two, and buy a robot welder by year three. I'd keep the plant job until the business pays me the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see the plan, but I don't know if the customers will still be there in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big firms with robots everywhere. If they can make a gate for half my price, why would anyone come to me? I'd have to be the local one who does custom work quickly and answers the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change anything with Ada?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ada and I want to get married in two years. I'd still do it. If the world's changing, I want to face it with my wife, not alone.

S3.say: Five years is enough to build something if you start now. I'd tell the younger ones at church to learn a trade and the tools together.
S3.think: Five years gives me time to do it properly: certificate, grow the gates business, then buy a robot once I've got customers to keep it busy.
S3.do: Gets a welding certificate in year one and moves the business to a small unit by year two. Buys a robot welder by year three. Keeps the plant job until the business pays the same.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with a clear plan but uncertainty about customers in 2031.
S3.quote: If the world's changing, I want to face it with my wife, not alone.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him sequence things properly, which clearly suits him. His real worry is competing with big automated firms, and his answer is being local and quick. Marriage to Ada stays on track as an anchor, not a casualty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone who wants to work. Build something, own something. I'd be a bit hard on people who waste it, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good about this one. Ten years is enough to have a proper workshop with robots doing the welding and me doing the customers and the designs. By 2036 I'd want to be the owner, not the worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the certificate, grow the business slowly, and put a fixed amount from every wage into it. I'd buy machines one at a time when the work justified them. And I'd buy a house with Ada in a few years, with a garage I can work from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This one's the opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see any risk in that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, yes. I'd probably say that when AGI can do almost everything, owning a small workshop doesn't make you safe. But owning something is better than owning nothing. That's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for the people you work with now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to hire a couple of the lads from the plant when it closes, even if robots do most of the welding. Someone has to install and deliver the gates. That's how communities work.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift for anyone who wants to work: build something and own something. I'd be a bit hard on people who waste it.
S4.think: I'd feel good about this one, with time for a proper workshop where robots weld and I handle customers and designs. By 2036 I'd want to be the owner, not the worker.
S4.do: Gets his certificate and grows the business slowly, putting a fixed amount from every wage into it. Buys machines one at a time as work justifies. Buys a house with Ada in a few years with a garage to work from.
S4.feel: Calm; he sees this as the opportunity.
S4.quote: By 2036 I'd want to be the owner, not the worker.
S4.fieldNote: The long warning reads as pure opportunity to him, though he admits owning a workshop doesn't make him safe from AGI. He plans to hire laid-off plant colleagues, a community-minded twist on his self-reliance. His hardness on people who 'waste it' is worth noting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have to bet my savings before I'm ready. What would help is cheap loans for small workshops to buy machines, and apprenticeships run by real businesses, not government schemes. And less paperwork for starting a business, it took me three months just to register.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my uncle. He's sixty, he taught me to weld, and he won't touch the AI. Whatever happens, I'll make sure his garage still has his name on the sign.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens, I'll make sure his garage still has his name on the sign.
portrait: Emeka is a 27-year-old junior press-line operator at a metal stamping plant, with a weekend welding business making garden gates in his uncle's garage and a girlfriend, Ada, who teaches primary school. He's traditional and free-market, churchgoing and self-reliant, and uses AI every day to quote, design and answer customers. He sees steady change and a ten-year warning as opportunities to own machines and become the boss, while fast AGI makes him anxious because he'd have to bet his savings before he's ready. His help for others runs through family, church and his own garage rather than government.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have to bet his savings on machines before he's ready.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small workshops to buy machines, apprenticeships run by real businesses, and less paperwork for starting a business.
